title: “BRIDEGROOM OF BLOOD”: THE NIGHT GOD CONFRONTED MOSES BEFORE HE COULD DELIVER ISRAEL
paragraphs: “BRIDEGROOM OF BLOOD”: THE NIGHT GOD CONFRONTED MOSES BEFORE HE COULD DELIVER ISRAEL

Three mysterious Hebrew words. A sharp stone. A terrified family. And a disturbing encounter in Exodus 4:25–26 that reveals why even the man chosen to confront Pharaoh could not afford to ignore the covenant of God.
What happens when the man God has chosen to deliver an entire nation is suddenly confronted by the very God who sent him?
Not by Pharaoh.
Not by an Egyptian soldier.
Not by some enemy hiding in the wilderness.
But by the LORD Himself.
And what makes this story even more unsettling is that Moses was not running away from his calling anymore.
He was finally obeying.
He had argued with God at the burning bush. He had questioned his ability to speak. He had pleaded for someone else to be sent. But now, after all his hesitation, Moses was on the road toward Egypt.
He was going where God told him to go.
And somewhere along that road, at a lodging place where his family should have been able to rest, something terrifying happened.
Scripture says:
“And it came to pass by the way in the inn, that the LORD met him, and sought to kill him.” — Exodus 4:24 (KJV)
Read that again.
The LORD met him.
And sought to kill him.
The same God who had appeared in the burning bush. The same God who had promised to be with Moses. The same God who was sending him to deliver His people.
Suddenly, Moses was facing a deadly encounter.
Then his wife, Zipporah, did something extraordinary.
She took a sharp stone, circumcised her son, touched his feet with the foreskin, and spoke words that have puzzled Bible readers for centuries.
“Surely a bloody husband art thou to me.” — Exodus 4:25 (KJV)
In Hebrew, the expression is:
חֲתַן־דָּמִים אַתָּה לִי
Chatan damim attah li.
Literally, something like:
“A bridegroom of blood you are to me.”
A bridegroom.
Of blood.
What could those words possibly mean?
Why would Zipporah say them?
Why was circumcision involved?
And why would God confront Moses so severely when Moses was finally doing what God had commanded?
The answer takes us into one of the most mysterious moments in the Old Testament.
But it also forces us to confront a question many Christians would rather avoid.
Can we be busy doing something for God while neglecting something God has already commanded?
Because before Moses could stand before Pharaoh and speak about covenant obedience, something within his own household needed attention.
And the road to Egypt became the place where that unfinished matter could no longer be ignored.
Imagine the scene.
The wilderness is dark.
The journey has been long.
Moses is traveling with his family toward a future filled with uncertainty. Egypt is waiting. Pharaoh is waiting. An enslaved nation is waiting.
Then the journey stops.
Scripture does not tell us exactly how the LORD confronted him. It does not describe a visible weapon, an angel, or a particular illness. It simply tells us that the encounter was deadly serious.
And somehow Zipporah understood that circumcision was involved.
There was no time for a lengthy discussion.
She took a flint.
Her son was circumcised.
Blood was shed.
And the immediate danger passed.
Exodus 4:26 says:
“So he let him go: then she said, A bloody husband thou art, because of the circumcision.” (KJV)
Three verses.
A handful of actions.
Almost no explanation.
Yet the theological weight of this encounter is enormous.
To understand why, we must travel backward from the road to Egypt to a much earlier conversation between God and Abraham.
In Genesis 17, the LORD established circumcision as the physical sign of His covenant with Abraham and his descendants.
God declared:
“This is my covenant, which ye shall keep, between me and you and thy seed after thee; Every man child among you shall be circumcised.” — Genesis 17:10 (KJV)
And in verse 14, the warning becomes severe.
The uncircumcised male who remained outside the covenant sign was to be cut off from his people because he had broken God's covenant.
Circumcision did not mean that a person had earned salvation.
It was not a magical ritual.
It was not proof that every circumcised heart was faithful to God.
It was a God-appointed sign of belonging to the covenant community.
And in the household of Abraham's descendants, it was not an optional cultural decoration.
It was a command.
Now consider Moses.
He was a descendant of Abraham.
He had been called by the covenant-keeping God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
He was being sent to announce the fulfillment of God's promises to Israel.
Yet Exodus 4 strongly indicates that the covenant sign had not been administered to one of his sons.
The passage does not explain why.
Perhaps there had been disagreement within the household. Perhaps the act had been delayed. Perhaps Moses had neglected the matter for reasons Scripture does not disclose.
We must not invent certainty where God has given us silence.
But the connection between the danger, Zipporah's circumcision of her son, and the release that followed is unmistakable.
The covenant sign mattered.
And its neglect had become a crisis.
Here is the uncomfortable truth.
A calling from God does not place anyone above obedience to God.
Moses could carry a shepherd's staff that God would use for miracles.
He could receive divine promises.
He could stand before kings.
He could become the human instrument through whom Israel would be delivered.
But none of those things made covenant faithfulness irrelevant.
And that should make every believer examine the distance between public ministry and private obedience.
Because it is possible to speak passionately about Scripture while refusing to let Scripture confront our own habits.
It is possible to encourage others to forgive while nurturing bitterness.
It is possible to defend marriage publicly while withholding tenderness and faithfulness at home.
It is possible to lead worship while privately resisting repentance.
It is possible to know the language of holiness without honestly dealing with the sin we have learned to hide.
Not every hardship is God's punishment.
Not every unanswered prayer reveals secret disobedience.
And we must never use this passage to terrify suffering believers into believing that God is trying to kill them.
But Exodus 4 does warn us against treating God's commands as though our religious activity could make obedience unnecessary.
Moses was not an ordinary traveler with an ordinary destination.
He was going to confront Pharaoh.
And what had God just instructed Moses to tell Pharaoh?
“Israel is my son, even my firstborn.” — Exodus 4:22 (KJV)
Then came a terrible warning.
If Pharaoh refused to release God's firstborn, Pharaoh's own firstborn would face judgment.
Do you see the literary connection?
Immediately after God speaks about His firstborn son, the narrative turns toward Moses, his household, and a covenant obligation involving his son.
The placement is difficult to dismiss.
Moses was about to announce the seriousness of God's covenant claims to Egypt.
Yet the covenant sign within his own household had been neglected.
The deliverer himself needed to reckon with the holiness of the God who was sending him.
And this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Because some of us want God to use us greatly while asking Him not to examine us closely.
We want the burning bush.
We want the calling.
We want the open doors.
We want the breakthrough.
We want to see chains fall and mountains move.
But we do not always want the light of God's Word entering the rooms of our lives we have kept locked.
The hidden resentment.
The secret compromise.
The dishonest transaction.
The apology we have delayed.
The relationship we know we need to make right.
The repentance we keep promising to begin tomorrow.
We may have become skilled at looking spiritually alive while quietly resisting the very truth we proclaim.
And sometimes the most merciful thing God can do is expose what we have refused to confront.
Not because He delights in our humiliation.
But because He is holy, and His truth is not a costume we wear when people are watching.
Now return to Zipporah.
She is often remembered only because of those strange words.
But the narrative gives her an extraordinary role.
While Moses is in danger, Zipporah acts.
The Hebrew text says she took a צֹר — tsor, a flint or sharp stone, and circumcised her son.
Then she touched the foreskin to his רַגְלָיו — raglav, literally “his feet.”
Whose feet?
The Hebrew does not explicitly identify the person.
Many interpreters understand them to be Moses' feet. Others recognize that the wording leaves room for discussion.
And there is another complication.
The Hebrew word raglayim, “feet,” can sometimes function as a euphemism in biblical language. Some scholars have therefore considered whether the expression carries a more intimate meaning.
But the passage does not settle that question.
Responsible interpretation must distinguish what the text actually says from what interpreters propose.
The same caution applies to the words “bridegroom of blood.”
The Hebrew noun חָתָן — chatan ordinarily refers to a bridegroom or a male relative by marriage.
The plural noun דָּמִים — damim means “blood” or “bloodshed,” depending on context.
The complete expression, chatan damim, is unusual.
It may reflect the language of marriage, kinship, or a ritual relationship associated with blood.
Some understand Zipporah's statement as an anguished expression directed toward Moses because circumcision had brought blood into their marriage.
Others suggest it may preserve an older expression whose precise significance is no longer fully recoverable.
The emotional tone is also uncertain.
Was she angry?
Terrified?
Relieved?
Reproachful?
Scripture does not tell us.
It would make a dramatic sermon to insist that she screamed those words in resentment.
It would make another dramatic sermon to insist that she whispered them in gratitude.
But neither claim can be proven from the passage.
What we know is enough.
Zipporah acted decisively in a moment of danger.
The circumcision was performed.
The deadly encounter ended.
And the text connects her unusual statement directly with the circumcision.
Sometimes faithful Bible reading requires us to say, “I do not know,” rather than turn an unanswered question into a sensational revelation.
Because Scripture is powerful enough without our exaggerations.
And the mystery itself carries a lesson.
We are not given every detail of what happened that night.
But we are shown that the God who called Moses was not a God whose holiness could be treated casually.
Yet there is something else here.
Something we must handle with extraordinary care.
Blood.
A covenant.
A threatened life.
A costly act.
A release from danger.
For Christians reading Exodus within the whole story of Scripture, these themes naturally direct our attention toward the greater work of redemption fulfilled in Jesus Christ.
But we must not confuse the two events.
Zipporah's act was the circumcision commanded under the Abrahamic covenant.
It was not the crucifixion of Christ.
Her son was not being offered as an atoning sacrifice.
And the phrase “bridegroom of blood” is not explicitly identified by Exodus as a prophecy about Jesus.
To claim otherwise would go beyond what the passage says.
Nevertheless, the wider biblical story reveals that covenant, blood, holiness, judgment, and redemption find their ultimate fulfillment in the saving work of Christ.
And here the contrast is breathtaking.
Moses was a servant called to deliver Israel from slavery.
Jesus is the greater Deliverer who saves His people from sin.
Moses was confronted by the seriousness of covenant obligation.
Jesus perfectly obeyed His Father.
Moses would later lead Israel through the waters of the sea.
Jesus passed through death and rose again, opening the way to everlasting life.
And while circumcision was the sign of the Abrahamic covenant, the New Testament reveals that the deepest human problem has always been more than an outward mark.
The heart itself needs transformation.
Long before Jesus came, Deuteronomy 30:6 spoke of the LORD circumcising the hearts of His people so that they would love Him.
The prophets continued to expose the tragedy of outward religion without inward faithfulness.
And Paul later wrote:

“For he is not a Jew, which is one outwardly; neither is that circumcision, which is outward in the flesh: But he is a Jew, which is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter.” — Romans 2:28–29 (KJV)
Paul was not declaring that ethnic identity or God's historical promises to Israel were meaningless.
He was confronting the false confidence that an outward religious sign could substitute for inward faithfulness before God.
Then in Colossians 2:11–12, he describes believers as having received a circumcision made without hands, connected with Christ's saving work and their union with Him, represented in baptism.
The point is not that Christians must undergo physical circumcision to be saved.
The New Testament explicitly rejects making circumcision a requirement for Gentile believers' justification.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by a physical operation, religious performance, or human merit.
And that is where the Gospel reaches the person who has spent years trying to look acceptable on the outside.
You can clean up your vocabulary and still carry hatred.
You can attend church and still be consumed by pride.
You can memorize verses and still refuse to forgive.
You can wear a cross and still avoid the One who died upon it.
You can appear disciplined, respectable, and spiritually mature while carrying wounds and sins you have never honestly brought before God.
But Jesus did not come merely to improve the appearance of religious people.
He came to save sinners.
To forgive the guilty.
To reconcile enemies to God.
To give life to those who cannot resurrect themselves.
And that includes the person reading this who has begun to wonder whether they have wandered too far.
Perhaps you used to pray without feeling ashamed.
Perhaps worship once felt natural.
Perhaps you remember a season when you were eager to open your Bible.
Then something happened.
A compromise became a habit.
A disappointment became bitterness.
A secret became a prison.
A failure became the name you started calling yourself.
And now, whenever you think about returning to God, you remember everything you have done.
You wonder whether Jesus would still receive you.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not promise that your sin is insignificant. It announces that Christ's mercy is greater than the debt you could never pay.
That is why the cross matters.
Not because God decided holiness was unimportant.
But because His holiness and His love meet in the saving work of His Son.
At Calvary, Jesus did not pretend that evil was harmless.
He bore the sins of His people.
He gave Himself willingly.
He died.
And on the third day, He rose again.
Peter wrote:

“Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold... But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.” — 1 Peter 1:18–19 (KJV, excerpt)
And Hebrews 9:22 reminds us that under the law, blood was central to purification and forgiveness.
The sacrifices of the old covenant pointed beyond themselves to the perfect and sufficient sacrifice of Jesus.
His blood is not one more ritual added to a long list of religious obligations.
His sacrifice is sufficient.
His resurrection is victorious.
His invitation to repent and believe is real.
Grace cannot be bought.
That truth must never be compromised.
Not even for a ministry we love.
Not even for a mission we believe in.
Not even when financial support could help the Gospel reach more people.
Because Jesus Christ is not a product.
Forgiveness is not a membership benefit.
It is God's gift to sinners who trust in His Son.
Yet grace does not leave us unchanged.
The same Jesus who receives sinners calls them to repentance.
The same Savior who forgives us calls us to follow Him.
And the same Gospel that frees us from earning God's acceptance also teaches us to live in grateful obedience.
That is why the story of Moses still matters.
It reminds us that being called by God is not permission to ignore His Word.
And it reminds us that the journey of faith must reach beyond public appearances into the ordinary, private places where our decisions reveal what we truly believe.
Maybe the most important thing you need to do after reading this is not to post a dramatic declaration.
Maybe it is to close your phone and pray.
Maybe it is to confess a sin you have defended for years.
Maybe it is to ask someone for forgiveness.
Maybe it is to stop excusing something Scripture has already confronted.
Maybe it is to return to Jesus after months of hiding behind religious appearances.
And maybe, for the first time in a long time, your prayer needs to be painfully simple.

“Lord Jesus, I have been trying to look faithful while hiding what needs Your mercy. I cannot save myself. Forgive me. Change my heart. Teach me to obey You, not to earn Your love, but because You loved me first.”
There is no shame in coming honestly to the Savior.
The shame is not greater than His cross.
The darkness is not stronger than His resurrection.
And the sin you confess is not a surprise to the One who already knows you completely.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
That promise is not an excuse to continue sinning.
It is an invitation to stop hiding.
And perhaps this is where the story of the “bridegroom of blood” finally reaches us.
Not by giving us a secret code about Moses.
Not by turning Zipporah into a symbol the Bible never identifies.
Not by pretending every unanswered question has an easy solution.
But by showing us how serious covenant faithfulness was, even in the household of God's appointed deliverer.
And then by directing our eyes toward the One greater than Moses.
Jesus Christ.
The One who did not merely speak about deliverance.
He accomplished it.
The One who did not need forgiveness for His own sins.
He gave Himself for ours.
The One whom the New Testament identifies as the Bridegroom who loves His people.
In Ephesians 5:25, Paul writes:
And in Revelation 19, the marriage supper of the Lamb becomes a picture of the final joy awaiting His redeemed people.
Notice the difference.
Exodus calls Moses a “bridegroom of blood” in a difficult and unusual expression spoken by Zipporah.
The New Testament presents Jesus as the Bridegroom who gives Himself for His people.
These are distinct biblical contexts, not identical titles.
But when we read the whole canon, we discover the astonishing beauty of a Savior whose covenant love was demonstrated through His own sacrifice.
He did not simply demand that His people become clean before approaching Him.
He gave Himself to cleanse them.
He did not wait for sinners to become worthy of His mercy.
He came to save the unworthy.
And He does not merely offer a better religious image.
He gives new life.
This is the heart of our message at Gospel Warrior.
Not because our scandals were harmless.
Not because our choices had no consequences.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because the risen Christ can redeem lives that sin, shame, and despair have devastated.
A broken marriage may require years of rebuilding trust.
A betrayed friendship may need honest confession and patient restoration.
An addiction may require accountability, treatment, and ongoing support.
Some consequences do not disappear overnight.
But even when restoration is difficult, the Gospel declares that our past does not have to be the final word about our standing before God.
Jesus Christ has the final word.
And that is a message worth carrying beyond this page.
Someone reading quietly may need to know that repentance and hope are still possible.
Not every person who reads a Christian article is ready to speak.
Some are grieving.
Some are ashamed.
Some are skeptical.
Some have been wounded by religious people.
Let us make the conversation a place of truth and compassion, not condemnation or pressure.

And if someone came to mind while you were reading, perhaps a brother, sister, parent, friend, struggling believer, or person who has quietly drifted away from church, consider tagging them with a personal word of encouragement.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to expose their struggles.
But to remind them that they have not been forgotten.
Someone may not know how to ask for prayer.
Someone may have been silently wondering whether there is any way back to God.
Return to Exodus 4:24–26.
Read Genesis 17.
Study Deuteronomy 30, Romans 2, Colossians 2, and Ephesians 5.
Do not merely remember the emotional force of the story.
Test its meaning against Scripture.
Because a powerful message should not leave you dependent on the writer.
It should make you hungry for the Word of God.

Our desire is to provide daily Scripture, biblical truth, Gospel-centered encouragement, conviction, healing, and practical discipleship that keeps pointing people to Jesus rather than to personalities.
And for those who want to walk with us more closely, there is another way to participate.
It does not replace the generosity and responsibilities you have toward your local church, and we would not claim that it automatically fulfills the biblical practice of tithing.

Rather, it is a voluntary monthly ministry contribution—an opportunity to give an additional offering toward the work of sharing biblical teaching, creating discipleship resources, and reaching more people with the Gospel.
Scripture teaches that Gospel ministry may receive material support. First Corinthians 9:14 speaks of those who proclaim the Gospel receiving their living from the Gospel.
Second Corinthians 9:7 also reminds us that giving should be willing, not compelled.
That matters deeply to us.
It can support the ongoing creation and sharing of articles, devotionals, biblical teaching, and discipleship materials.
It can help make Gospel-centered resources available to people who may never be able to contribute financially themselves.
And it can allow those who are able to give to participate in serving those who cannot.
These free resources are part of our commitment to make spiritual nourishment more accessible.
It is not the heart of the invitation.
The heart is discipleship.
The heart is helping people understand Scripture.
The heart is seeing more people hear about repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through Jesus Christ.
The Gospel belongs to Christ.
The glory belongs to God.
And every act of service must remain subject to His Word.
Before you leave, think again about Moses.
A man who had heard God's voice.
A man who had received an extraordinary calling.
A man who was on his way to confront the greatest political power of his world.
And yet, on an obscure road, in a brief and frightening encounter, he was reminded that the God who sends His servants is also the God who calls them to faithfulness.
We do not know every detail of what happened at that lodging place.
We do not know every emotion Zipporah felt.
We cannot confidently reconstruct every movement, every word, or every unanswered question.
But we know this:
The LORD's covenant was not something Moses could simply overlook.
And today, under the new covenant, we know something even more wonderful.
The Savior who calls us to repent is the Savior who died and rose again to save us.
He does not ask us to purchase His mercy.
He calls us to receive Him by faith.
He does not invite us to maintain a polished religious disguise.
He calls us into the light.
And He does not promise that following Him will be painless.
He promises something infinitely greater than a comfortable life.
He gives Himself.
So do not walk away from this passage merely fascinated by three strange Hebrew words.
Walk away asking whether the God who sees your public worship also has your private obedience.
Walk away remembering that no ministry assignment is greater than the Lord who gives it.
Walk away with renewed gratitude that Jesus Christ has accomplished the redemption no sinner could ever accomplish alone.
And if you have been hiding, come to Him.
If you have been compromising, repent.
If you have been despairing, look again to the crucified and risen Savior.
If you have been pretending, tell Him the truth.
Because the greatest miracle is not that God can make a religious person look impressive.
It is that He can take a guilty sinner, forgive them through Christ, and begin making them new.
The road where Moses was confronted by God's holiness reminds us that the only safe place for a sinner is not behind a religious reputation, but in the mercy of Jesus Christ.
